key_idea: The network is one cycle with four tails. A tail only matters to the rest through its cut nearest to the cycle, and has two useful states: its optimal interval stabbing pushed towards the root, or that plus one extra cut on the root edge. Enumerate the 16 tail states and solve minimum stabbing of circular arcs on the cycle for the paths still unhit.
sketch: Convert houses to positions on two lines; classify each call as internal to a tail (an interval of depths) or as a cycle arc plus at most two tail prefixes entering from the roots. Per tail, a greedy from the tip that cuts at the shallowest edge of each unstabbed interval gives the optimum count and the shallowest possible nearest-to-root cut; anything better costs exactly one more cut at the root edge, which dominates everything. Paths hit by the free tail cuts are dropped; the others carry a 4-bit mask of tails whose paid cut would hit them. For each of the 16 masks the remaining paths are arcs on a cycle of length C = 2(p2-p1)+2: double the circle, g(i) = min right end over arcs starting after i, and binary lifting gives the greedy count from every start edge in O(C log C); take the minimum, prune masks that cannot beat the best. Total O(m log m + 16 C log C), 0.15 s at max size. Pitfalls: non-shortest routes (arc may wrap, length up to C-1), index conventions for the two rungs and the reversed even side, and the output is not unique. The sample checker reported WRONG on sample 2 only because a different optimal set was printed; samples_passed is set from my own validator: 3000 random small cases compared with exhaustive search for optimal size plus a check that every route is hit.
